\chapter{Which One: By Colour, Size And Shape}
\label{ch:el-color-y-el-tamano}
\hlchaptermodality{358}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el color, el tamano, la forma, la clase and la marca, and single out one thing from several without pointing at it.}

Complete ES-C358-marca: single out one thing among several by its colour, its size, its shape, its kind and its maker.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el color]{el color — a covering, and the hiding under it}

\label{lesson:ES-C358-color}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the present}, then \emph{the card}. (\emph{El regalo}; \emph{la tarjeta}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item rojo — one answer to it.
  \item verde — another.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ko-LOR}, two beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{l} is clear and forward, never swallowed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el color} — \textquotedblleft{}the colour.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{cēlāre} is to hide, and \textbf{color} is built on it. A colour is the coat over a surface — the thing that stops you seeing what the surface is actually made of. To a Roman, painting something was covering it up.

The hiding is scattered through English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to \textbf{conceal} is to hide, with the Latin verb almost intact;
  \item an \textbf{occult} thing is a covered one;
  \item a \textbf{cell} and a \textbf{cellar} are places to hide things, from \emph{cella}, a store room;
  \item a \textbf{helmet} hides a head, and \textbf{hull} is what covers a seed.
\end{itemize}

And then the good one. English \textbf{hell} is the same ancient root, arriving down the Germanic road rather than the Latin one — the \emph{covered} place, the hidden place, before any theology was attached to it. Latin \emph{c} comes out as Germanic \emph{h}, which is the swap you already met standing between \emph{cien} and \textbf{hundred}.

Once you have \emph{el color}, you can pick one thing out of five without pointing at it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five ways to single out one thing among several.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el color}
  \item \emph{¿de qué color?}
  \item \emph{el color rojo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{cēlāre} mean? (To hide.) And what Latin sound turns into an English \emph{h}? (A \emph{c}, as in \emph{cien} and hundred.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el tamaño]{el tamaño — \emph{so big}, welded into a noun}

\label{lesson:ES-C358-tamano}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the card}, then \emph{the colour}. (\emph{La tarjeta}; \emph{el color}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item grande — one answer to it.
  \item también — where its first half is hiding.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ta-MA-ño}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{ñ} is the \emph{n}-with-a-\emph{y} sound. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el tamaño} — \textquotedblleft{}the size.\textquotedblright{}

Two Latin words, hammered flat. \textbf{Tam magnum} is \textquotedblleft{}so big,\textquotedblright{} and Spanish welded it into one word.

It was an adjective first. \emph{Un tamaño error} meant \textquotedblleft{}an error that big,\textquotedblright{} and you can still meet it in older writing. Then people kept asking \emph{¿de qué tamaño?} — \textquotedblleft{}of what so-big?\textquotedblright{} — and the answer hardened into a noun. Spanish now uses it for size the way English uses a word borrowed from French.

Both halves are worth having on their own.

\textbf{Tam} is the \emph{tan} you already own. \textbf{También} is \emph{tan bien}, \textquotedblleft{}so well,\textquotedblright{} which slid into \textquotedblleft{}also.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Tampoco} is \emph{tan poco}, \textquotedblleft{}so little,\textquotedblright{} which slid into \textquotedblleft{}neither.\textquotedblright{} The same little word, three times.

\textbf{Magnus}, great, is the \emph{magn-} in English \textbf{magnify}, \textbf{magnitude}, \textbf{magnificent} and \textbf{magnate}, the \emph{ma-} in \textbf{major} and \textbf{maximum}, and the \emph{mas-} in \textbf{master}, who is the greater one. Spanish has it in \emph{magno} — as in Alejandro Magno.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The second way to single a thing out, and a Latin pair you have been using in two other words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el tamaño}
  \item \emph{¿de qué tamaño?}
  \item \emph{un tamaño grande}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin words are inside \emph{tamaño}? (\emph{Tam} and \emph{magnum} — so big.) And which word you know already carries the same \emph{tam}? (\emph{También}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la forma]{la forma — one Latin word that arrived twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C358-forma}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the colour}, then \emph{the size}. (\emph{El color}; \emph{el tamaño}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cosa — what has one.
  \item f $\to$ h — the change that gave it a twin.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FOR-ma}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la forma} — \textquotedblleft{}the shape,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the form.\textquotedblright{}

This word came into Spanish twice, and the two arrivals do not look alike.

The short road is the one you can see. \textbf{Forma} was borrowed out of Latin books with nothing changed at all, and it means shape. English borrowed it the same way and built a shelf from it: \textbf{form}, \textbf{formal}, \textbf{format}, \textbf{formula}, \textbf{uniform}, \textbf{transform}, \textbf{reform}, \textbf{conform}.

The long road is the good one. Latin \textbf{formōsus} meant \textquotedblleft{}well shaped.\textquotedblright{} It came down through mouths rather than books, and words that did that turned their Latin \emph{f} into a Spanish \emph{h} — \emph{facere} to \emph{hacer}, \emph{fabulari} to \emph{hablar}. Do it to \emph{formōsus} and you get \textbf{hermoso}, which no longer means shapely. It means beautiful.

So \emph{la forma} and \emph{hermoso} are the same Latin word, and the difference between them is eight hundred years of being said out loud.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The third way to single a thing out, and a doublet with the same root at both ends.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la forma}
  \item \emph{la forma de la mesa}
  \item \emph{el color y la forma}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{formōsus} mean in Latin? (Well shaped.) And what does its Spanish descendant \emph{hermoso} mean now? (Beautiful.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la clase]{la clase — six bands of Romans, sorted by money}

\label{lesson:ES-C358-clase}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the size}, then \emph{the shape}. (\emph{El tamaño}; \emph{la forma}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el tipo — the word standing beside it.
  \item cl-, pl-, fl- $\to$ ll- — the change this word escaped.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KLA-se}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{cl} stays a hard \emph{k} plus \emph{l}, both sounded. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la clase} — \textquotedblleft{}the class,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the kind,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}the lesson.\textquotedblright{}

Rome counted its citizens every five years and sorted them into \textbf{classēs} by what they owned. There were six, and where you stood decided what armour you brought to war and how much your vote weighed.

A writer good enough to belong at the top was \textbf{classicus} — first class. That is where English \textbf{classic} comes from, and it is worth knowing that the word never meant \emph{old}. It meant \emph{top band}. A classic film made last year is being called first-rate, not ancient.

Spanish uses \textbf{la clase} for three things at once: the social band, the kind of thing, and the room where a lesson happens.

One sound to notice. A word that came down through mouths and started \emph{cl-} usually comes out of Spanish as \emph{ll-}: Latin \emph{clamāre} gave \emph{llamar}, \emph{plēnus} gave \emph{lleno}, \emph{flamma} gave \emph{llama}. \textbf{Clase} kept its \emph{cl-} untouched, and that is the fingerprint of a word that came in from books instead.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fourth way to single a thing out, and the difference between a word that was said and one that was read.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la clase}
  \item \emph{¿qué clase de queso?}
  \item \emph{una clase de cosa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{classicus} mean? (Of the top band, first class.) And what usually happens to an inherited Spanish word that starts \emph{cl-}? (It comes out as \emph{ll-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la marca]{la marca — a boundary before it was a sign}

\label{lesson:ES-C358-marca}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the shape}, then \emph{the kind}. (\emph{La forma}; \emph{la clase}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el nombre — what it sits next to.
  \item la huella — a mark of a different kind.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MAR-ka}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} before the \emph{c} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la marca} — \textquotedblleft{}the mark,\textquotedblright{} and then \textquotedblleft{}the brand.\textquotedblright{}

The Germanic \textbf{marka} was a boundary first. Not a sign — an edge, the line where one people's land stopped and another's began. The sign came second: the stone, the cut in a tree, the thing you put there so the edge could be seen.

From the boundary meaning:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{march} is a border land, which is why the country between England and Wales is the Welsh \textbf{Marches};
  \item the lord who held one was a \textbf{marquis}, ranked above a count because a border is harder to hold than a middle;
  \item and \textbf{Denmark} is the mark of the Danes.
\end{itemize}

From the sign meaning: English \textbf{mark}, to \textbf{remark} (to mark a thing again, out loud), and to \textbf{demarcate}. Latin had a cousin, \textbf{margō}, an edge, which gives \textbf{margin} — the boundary of a page.

Spanish \textbf{la marca} kept both. It is the mark on a thing, and then the maker who put it there: the brand. So asking \emph{¿de qué marca?} is asking whose sign is on it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways to single a thing out without pointing: \emph{el color}, \emph{el tamaño}, \emph{la forma}, \emph{la clase}, \emph{la marca}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la marca}
  \item \emph{¿de qué marca?}
  \item \emph{el color, el tamaño, la forma y la clase}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{marka} before it was a sign? (A boundary.) And why does a marquis outrank a count? (He held a border.)
\end{tcolorbox}
